transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-06-25 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~48 mins | Attendees: Maya, Omar (Redwood); Jared, Priya, Marco, Leah (Silverridge)

Summary: High-level discovery on p95 targets, concurrency for streaming product (chat + summarization), exploring hosted vs dedicated vs private for throughput economics and data control. Customer cares about 200ms p95 for short completions and steady 100+ concurrent streaming sessions at peak.

Topics: p95 targets, streaming latency per token, concurrency, token/sec benchmarks, KV cache behavior, private deployment / KMS / audit log requirements, pilot scope.

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE, with Omar our SE. How's everyone?
[00:06] Jared Blake: Hey Maya, thanks, yeah all good. Quick note, sorry if my audio is a bit low, I'm on a bad mic.
[00:10] Maya Chen: no worries, we can lean in. Quick agenda, we'll ask about current workloads, targets, latency SLOs, and then we'll talk about hosting options and next steps. Omar will jump in with numbers.
[00:22] Omar Patel: Hi, hi. I'll try to pull some numbers live but I'll mostly talk off our benchmark experience, ok?
[00:27] Priya Singh: Great — our product is a real-time summarization widget embedded in client apps. We do streaming token-by-token updates so user sees partial summaries. Typical short request is 60 tokens in prompt, and target reply is 120 tokens. p95 is the big one for us.
[00:40] Marco Ruiz: We get spikes in traffic when reports publish, so for planning we want steady 100 concurrent streaming clients and spikes to 300 for maybe 10-20 minutes. Cost is also a hard constraint.
[00:52] Maya Chen: That's helpful. When you say p95 target, do you mean end-to-end time to first token, or p95 tail for full completion?
[00:59] Priya Singh: Mostly to first token for perceived interactivity; full completion can be slower but still want reasonable tail — first token ideally ~200-300ms p95.
[01:09] Omar Patel: Okay so 200-300ms to first token p95 for streaming. That's tight but doable depending on model size, quantization, and deployment mode. A few clarifying q's: what models are you planning to run? Are they base open weights or a fine-tuned variant?
[01:24] Priya Singh: We use a fine tuned 7B for summarization and a 13B for longer contextual stuff. They are based on LlaMA derivatives; we've pruned and tuned in-house.
[01:34] Maya Chen: Good. Hosted vs dedicated vs private — what sort of data residency / encryption requirements do you have?
[01:40] Jared Blake: We'll need encryption-at-rest with customer KMS for production, plus audit logs. For the pilot we can use hosted but eventually likely require private VPC or dedicated with KMS. Also SOC2 is a must.
[01:50] Omar Patel: Redwood supports KMS integrations and audit logs for Dedicated and Private; Hosted can be arranged with managed encryption keys but many customers prefer Dedicated/Private for KMS. We can share our SOC2 report.
[01:59] Leah Park: timeline wise we want a pilot in July and hope to decide by EOY. If the numbers line up and reliability is there we can go dedicated.
[02:08] Marco Ruiz: Quick infra note — we currently run inference on spot GPU clusters for internal models, but for customer-facing we need guaranteed SLOs.
[02:16] Omar Patel: Right. For SLOs you likely want Dedicated pools. We'll talk about continuous batching, KV cache warm-up and how that impacts p95. For streaming the key is minimizing cold path and avoiding cross-tenant noisy neighbor issues.
[02:31] Maya Chen: Omar, can you frame expected token/sec and latency per GPU for their model sizes so they can map to concurrency?
[02:36] Omar Patel: Sure. From our internal benchmarks: for a tuned 7B with 120 token output, on a single high-end A100 or equivalent with optimized kernels and fp16/4-bit quant, you might see ~350-600 tokens/sec steady if you're running full throughput and using batching. For 13B it's closer to 150-300 tokens/sec depending on quant and sequence length. But streaming first token latency depends on request routing and KV cache — if you have prefix cache hits you can hit 100-200ms first token in dedicated setups. Hosted will add tiny extra network hop but typically stays within 150-300ms if model is warm.
[03:18] Priya Singh: those are rough numbers we can work with. For the 7B, if we want 100 concurrent streaming users with average output 120 tokens that's roughly 100 * 120 = 12k tokens in flight, and at 400 tokens/sec per GPU that's ~30 GPUs sustained? My math maybe off.
[03:36] Omar Patel: Quick calc — 100 concurrent clients each streaming 120 tokens but they're streamed, that doesn't multiply linearly because tokens/sec is throughput; 100 concurrent at 400 tok/s per GPU means one GPU can service 400 tokens per second; if each user emits 120 tokens at 10 seconds duration, the concurrency window matters. I can build a spreadsheet for exact sizing with your distribution.
[03:52] Jared Blake: yes please send the sizing calc. We need both steady-state and burst sizing — we can tolerate a bit of queuing but p95 cannot spike above 500ms to first token or user complaints rise.
[04:03] Maya Chen: noted. On caching: do you have many repeated prefixes or similar contexts? That changes the KV hit profile.
[04:08] Priya Singh: some repeating, yes. Many clients use same system prompts. We do per-customer personalization though.
[04:13] Omar Patel: Good. With prefix caching you can cut compute considerably. Redwood supports automatic prefix/KV caching at the serving layer; for dedicated or private you can control cache retention to align with your user patterns. One caveat: cache warm-up on spike events is the main source of tail latency.
[04:27] Marco Ruiz: For pilot we need to simulate bursts — do you have tooling to replay our traffic shape?
[04:31] Omar Patel: We do — our SEs can run a replay harness against a sandboxed cluster. We'll need sample traces (timestamps, req sizes) from you. That was one of the action items.
[04:40] Maya Chen: let's capture benchmarks to show delta between hosted/dedicated/private. Any questions on compliance?
[04:47] Leah Park: yes, for private on-prem we need details on upgrade cadence and support windows. Also can you do air-gapped installs?
[04:54] Omar Patel: We offer a private deployment package; air-gapped installs are done via our on-prem bundle but require SOW; upgrade cadence is customer controlled, we provide patch bundles. We'll send the deployment checklist.
[05:04] Jared Blake: thanks. Also curious about failover — we can't have global outages; if a region loses capacity do you do model fallback to a smaller variant?
[05:13] Omar Patel: Yes, smart routing and fallback is part of Redwood: policy-based routing to variants, region fallback, and automatic scaling with warm standby pools. But fallback to a smaller model will change quality; we usually recommend explicit canaries.
[05:25] Priya Singh: on the quality note — we need to run evals to compare 7B to 13B and quantized variants so we don't regress summarization quality.
[05:33] Omar Patel: Good point — Redwood Optimize can help with quantization recommendations and quality monitoring tied to prompt sets. We can run quick evals in pilot.
[05:41] Maya Chen: let's go back to p95 math and an example scenario: assume 7B, dedicated pool, we want 200ms p95 first token and sustained 100 conc. Omar?
[05:51] Omar Patel: To get 200ms p95 to first token you'd need warm model and sticky routing, minimized serialization. For 100 concurrent streams, if each stream's first token arrives within the first 500ms window, the infrastructure needs to have reserved capacity to prevent queuing. Typically that means provisioning to handle 100 concurrent steady-state with small headroom — likely 10-15 GPUs depending on kernel perf and batching; again I'll provide an exact spreadsheet.
[06:14] Marco Ruiz: 10-15 GPUs for 100 conc sounds optimistic, but maybe if tokens/sec high. We'll need numbers.
[06:20] Omar Patel: I'll capture the assumptions — token length, average token generation rate, request inter-arrival distribution, and batching policy.
[06:28] Maya Chen: another practical question — in hosted mode, how do you expose metrics? We want token-level tracing and latency per route.
[06:34] Omar Patel: Redwood Console provides per-route latency, token counts, trace ids, and you can export to Prometheus or our API. For Dedicated and Private you can push logs to your SIEM.
[06:44] Priya Singh: Security: we need SAML SSO for console, RBAC, field-level redaction on logs. Is that supported?
[06:51] Omar Patel: Yes SAML + RBAC supported for Dedicated/Private; hosted supports SSO for enterprise customers. Field redaction is available for logs and we can show the audit log format.
[06:59] Leah Park: back to cost: how does dedicated pricing differ from hosted? We prefer committed capacity if it reduces unit price.
[07:06] Maya Chen: dedicated is reserved capacity with a commit; pricing is lower per token in exchange for reservation. Hosted is pay-as-you-go at a higher price but no commit. We'll send example price bands.
[07:16] Jared Blake: For procurement we will need an approximate TCO for 12 months at expected scale, include infra and Redwood fees.
[07:23] Maya Chen: we will include that in the spreadsheet.
[07:26] (long pause / typing sounds)
[07:32] Priya Singh: quick nerd question — how do you handle KV cache consistency for per-tenant personalization? We can't have cross-tenant leakage.
[07:39] Omar Patel: Cache is tenant-isolated. The KV cache is per-model-instance and per-tenant, no cross-tenant sharing. For Private/Dedicated you can control cache eviction policy and size.
[07:50] Marco Ruiz: what's the cold-start behavior after model restarts? Our jobs sometimes evict old models from memory under heavy churn.
[07:58] Omar Patel: Cold starts are the painful bit — when model isn't resident we see first-token latencies in the seconds range. We recommend warm pools and preloading for production. If you're using Dedicated, you pin a small warm set; we can do auto-warm heuristics.
[08:13] Maya Chen: question for Priya — do you run long context windows often? That affects memory and kernel selection.
[08:18] Priya Singh: sometimes yes, for long reports we keep up to 8k context. But streaming short summaries are the majority.
[08:23] Omar Patel: 8k context pushes memory needs and tends to reduce tok/sec. For those requests you might pair with the 13B and route shorter contexts to 7B.
[08:32] Jared Blake: we like routing by policy — latency vs quality. Can Redwood do per-route static policy?
[08:38] Omar Patel: Yes, you can define route policies — latency-priority, cost-priority, and Redwood can auto-fallback.
[08:44] Leah Park: about pilot acceptance criteria — what should we test in the first two weeks so we can sign off?
[08:50] Maya Chen: typically: 1) p95 to first token under pilot trace at or below target (200-500ms), 2) no functional regressions vs current summary quality, 3) stability under simulated burst 3x expected peak, 4) KMS + audit log verification.
[09:03] Priya Singh: OK that sounds reasonable.
[09:07] Omar Patel: For the pilot we'll stand up a sandbox dedicated pool, run replayed traffic, and run the eval set. We will instrument logs and provide traces.
[09:16] Marco Ruiz: Can we see a comparison between quantized 7B and full fp16 13B in terms of latency and quality?
[09:23] Omar Patel: Absolutely, we'll produce a short matrix: latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, and quality delta for a few prompts.
[09:31] (slight crosstalk)
[09:34] Jared Blake: procurement question — do you support SOC2 + custom DPA and addendum for data residency?
[09:40] Maya Chen: yes, we have templates and can negotiate addenda for enterprise customers. We'll share our legal pack.
[09:46] Leah Park: and on support SLAs? We will need 24/7 for production.
[09:50] Omar Patel: Enterprise tiers include 24/7 on-call and runbooks, plus playbooks for failover.
[09:56] Priya Singh: quick follow-up — when you say 150-600 tokens/sec per GPU, do those numbers include streaming overhead for per-token flushes?
[10:04] Omar Patel: The wide band includes streaming overhead. If you're using small step sizes (e.g., send every token) it's slightly lower because of more RPCs; batching the token flushes every 4-8 tokens reduces overhead. But user perceived interactivity sometimes demands per-token. There's a tradeoff.
[10:18] Marco Ruiz: tradeoff is clear. We may batch a bit to improve throughput but keep first token latency low.
[10:24] Maya Chen: ok recording checkpoints. We'll send the following: pricing, sizing spreadsheet, SOC2 and KMS docs, deployment checklist, and propose pilot dates.
[10:34] Priya Singh: can Omar include recommended autoscale policy? For bursts we need quick ramp-up.
[10:39] Omar Patel: yes, autoscale policies with warm standby, burst capacity, and queue thresholds. I'll include a recommended baseline and conservative/aggressive bands.
[10:47] Jared Blake: good. Also include per-route tracing examples and sample dashboard screenshots if possible.
[10:52] Maya Chen: will do. Any final items?
[10:55] Leah Park: just to confirm, we'll share sample traffic trace and eval prompts by Friday.
[10:59] Jared Blake: yes, we'll try to get that to you.
[11:02] Maya Chen: perfect. Thanks all, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and SOW.
[11:06] (hangouts noise)

Notes on transcription: there are a few missed words near 03:30 where background noise clipped one attendee; some proper nouns (LLM names) may be slightly off in automated transcript (eg LLaMA variants sometimes transcribed as Llima).

Recap / explicit next steps (verbatim):
- Omar to deliver token/sec baseline + sizing spreadsheet and autoscale recommendation (due 2027-07-02).
- Maya to send pricing + pilot SOW + SOC2/KMS docs (due 2027-06-28).
- Silverridge (Jared) to share traffic traces and eval prompts (due 2027-06-30).
- Schedule pilot week (target week of 2027-07-11) once traces received.

End of transcript.
